common_name: Quickpick Pinkeye Cowpea (Compact Top-Set Purple Hull Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably above 65F; determinate, erect habit holds pods high above the compact ~20-inch canopy, making it easy to spot and hand-pick in a home garden row.

directions: Quickpick was released by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station as a compact pinkeye purple hull type bred for resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus. Pods are dark purple, 7-8 inches long, and set simultaneously at the top of the plant, giving the variety its name and making a single harvest pass practical. Seeds are cream colored with a large maroon eye, larger than older purple hull standards, and cook up with classic pinkeye flavor. Matures quickly at around 60 days, making it useful for a second planting later in the Gulf Coast summer.

common_name: Ogle Southern Pea (Clemson-Bred Purple Hull Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; a bushy, short-runnered purple hull type that holds pods upright for easier hand harvest.

directions: Ogle was bred by longtime Clemson horticulturist Roy (W.L.) Ogle, the same breeder behind the classic Colossus and Hercules southern peas, and was released commercially by Clemson University decades after he first developed the line. It is a purple hull type selected for a large eating seed, strong yield, and resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus, a disease that has historically limited purple hull production in humid climates. Like other purple hull peas it can be picked green for fresh shelling or left to dry fully for storage peas.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; a semi-erect, short-runnered bush with straight pods held above the foliage for easy shelling.

directions: Hercules was released in 1981 by the Clemson Agricultural Experiment Station, bred by longtime breeder Roy Ogle. It is a large-seeded crowder type with straight 8-9 inch pods held upright on a bushy, short-runnered plant, and coffee-colored crowder seed that shells easily. Matures around 75 days, later than most bush purple hull types, rewarding the wait with an especially large, meaty pea. Best suited to gardeners who want a heavier-seeded crowder flavor distinct from cream or blackeye types.

common_name: Carolina Crowder Southern Pea (Disease-Resistant Heirloom Crowder Cowpea)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; forms large, bushy plants and is easy to shell by hand.

directions: Carolina Crowder is a classic Southern crowder pea selected and maintained by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange, updated over time for broader Fusarium wilt resistance while keeping its old-fashioned flavor. Pods are straw colored with a purple tint, 7-9 inches long, and packed tightly with light-brown crowder-type seeds that shell out easily. Large, prolific, bushy plants make it a reliable choice for a big drying-pea harvest, ready in about 61 days to first picking.

common_name: Creel Crowder Southern Pea (Alabama Family Heirloom Crowder Cowpea)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; give this semi-vining crowder a bit more row space than bush-type peas.

directions: Creel Crowder is a family heirloom traced to R.E. Creel, a truck farmer in Warrior, Alabama in the 1930s, and preserved through Southern Exposure Seed Exchange. Its semi-vining plants produce curved 6-inch pods that turn golden yellow as they dry, filled with large brown crowder seeds. Very productive for a heritage variety, it reaches first harvest around 61 days and is well suited to both fresh shelling and dry storage.

common_name: Washday Southern Pea (Quick-Cooking Tennessee Heirloom Cowpea)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; half-runner vines benefit from a bit of extra spacing or light support.

directions: Washday is an old-time Tennessee heirloom southern pea, so named because its small cream-colored seeds with dark hilums cooked up quickly enough to fit into a busy laundry day. Half-runner vines set clusters of 3-4 pods, each 5-6 inches long, for relatively easy picking despite the vining habit. It is now a rare, at-risk heirloom, listed among threatened Place-Based Foods of Appalachia varieties, making it a good conservation choice for gardeners wanting to keep an old regional pea in circulation.

common_name: Arkansas Blackeye #1 Cowpea (Early Commercial Blackeye Southern Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; this medium bush with no basal runners suits conventional row spacing.

directions: Arkansas Blackeye #1 was the first blackeye-type southern pea released specifically for commercial production in Arkansas, developed through the University of Arkansas cowpea breeding program. It forms a medium-sized bush, 20-26 inches tall with no basal runners, suited to conventional or narrow-row planting. Seeds carry a distinct, medium-sized black eye similar to California Blackeye No. 5, and the variety matures a few days earlier than Coronet or Pinkeye Purple Hull-BVR, typically 60-70 days from sowing.
sources: University of Arkansas cowpea breeding program

common_name: Chinese Red Ripper Cowpea (Small-Seeded Bushy Red Ripper Type)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; heat tolerant enough to succession-sow through the hottest part of a Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Chinese Red Ripper, also sold as Chinese Red, is a smaller-seeded, bushier selection of the classic Red Ripper cowpea. It is highly heat tolerant, blooms and sets pods early, and produces long 12-14 inch pods holding 18-21 seeds each, making it a heavy producer for a bush-type pea. It works equally well as a fresh green-shelled pea, a dried storage pea, or a summer cover crop and wildlife forage planting.

common_name: Dimpled Brown Crowder Pea (Bush-Type Flattened Crowder Cowpea)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; a prolific bush type that yields large pods well suited to freezing, canning, or drying.

directions: Dimpled Brown Crowder is a bush-type southern pea whose seeds are packed so tightly in the pod that they take on a flattened, dimpled shape, the classic crowder trait. Large pods each hold 12-15 seeds, and plants are prolific yielders good for freezing, canning, or drying. Fresh green-shell shellies can be picked well before the roughly 80 days needed for fully dry pods, giving a long harvest window from one planting.

common_name: Florida Conch Pea, Bush (Small White-Seeded North Florida Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed in full sun; this is the bush-type strain, selected later from the originally vining conch pea.

directions: Florida Conch is a now-rare southern pea that arrived in north Florida in the late 1800s, likely from the West Indies, and became prized for its tiny white seeds, delicate texture, and short cooking time. The original conch pea was a vining plant, and a vining strain still exists, but this bush-type selection was developed later as vining peas fell out of favor for home gardens. Green-shell shellies are ready in about 63 days, with fully dry peas following around 70 days, and the mild, delicate flavor sets it apart from heartier crowder and blackeye types.
